items.intro: Searching how to blur background on iPhone usually leads to Portrait mode. That path only works at capture time, on supported cameras, and only if you remembered to turn it on. If the photo is already in Recents, you need an editor that can blur the background after you shoot.
items.definition: How to blur background on iPhone after capture means keeping the subject sharp while softening everything behind it on a photo that already exists. How to Blur Photo (Make Blur) is an iPhone app for that job: subject detection, intensity control, and on-device processing on iOS 17.1 or later.
items.image_alt: How to Blur Photo keeping a subject sharp while the background goes soft

sections.heading: Why Portrait mode is not the same job
paragraphs: iPhone Portrait mode records depth when you press the shutter. If the shot was taken in Photo mode, or the person stepped out of the depth range, Photos has nothing to refocus. Markup can scribble over a background, but that is not a photographic blur.

A dedicated blur app fills that gap: you open the existing image, the subject is separated, and you choose how strong the background goes. That is the search intent behind how to blur background on iPhone for most people who land here from Google—not a camera tutorial.

sections.heading: What you need
paragraphs: An iPhone running iOS 17.1 or later, the How to Blur Photo app (free to download; advanced styles are optional in-app purchases), and a photo in Recents. No internet is required to process the blur—the listing states images stay on the device.

paragraphs: Use background blur when the subject should stay identifiable: a face, a pet, a plate of food, a product. If you need a transparent cutout for a shop template, that is background removal—a different product category.
Social posts and portraits are the listing’s stated use cases. The app is built around one job: blur photo backgrounds with the subject held.

paragraphs: Gaussian is even and calm. Motion has a heading: left-right for a runner, mild for a cyclist, stronger for a night street. If the photo is a seated portrait, gaussian or bokeh-style looks are usually more honest than fake speed.
The App Store listing calls out action shots as a use case. Match the effect to the picture you have, not to the keyword alone.

sections.heading: Gaussian vs motion vs pixel
paragraphs: Gaussian: even, photographic, good for portraits and products. Motion: directional, for action. Pixelate/mosaic: privacy or graphic looks, not a lens simulation. Crystalize and ghosting are creative, not a stand-in for a fast prime.
If you searched only “gaussian blur,” start here, then branch to motion or face blur if that was the real job.

sections.heading: Apple Photos Clean Up vs this app
paragraphs: iOS 18 Clean Up can pixelate faces, but only on Apple Intelligence hardware (iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 class, plus the software that supports it). Many phones that can run iOS 17.1 cannot use that filter. Markup rectangles look amateur on a feed.

If your iPhone is not in the Intelligence set, or Clean Up keeps removing the whole head, a dedicated face-blur tool is the reliable path. Blur, then share; do not rely on a platform’s “only me” setting.

sections.heading: Do it before you send
paragraphs: Once an unblurred original leaves your phone, you cannot pull it back. Apply face blur, save a copy, and send the copy. Keep the original in a private album if you still need it.
